meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>nine</radical> radical and the <kanji>nine</kanji> kanji are the same character, so this one lands in your memory for free.

reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine a young monk called <reading>Zen</reading> keeps trying to paint one flawless circle in a single brushstroke. reading_mnemonic: Once a month the night janitor at Sei's school, a man called <reading>Getz</reading>, mops the echoing hallway by the light of the full moon. meaning_mnemonic: You already know the <radical>fire</radical> radical, and the <kanji>fire</kanji> kanji is that same upright log with sparks flicking off both sides.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>gold</radical> radical and the <kanji>gold</kanji> kanji are the very same character, which also came to mean money because for centuries gold coins were exactly what people paid with.

meaning_mnemonic: You met this shape already as the <radical>earth</radical> radical, and the <kanji>earth</kanji> kanji is the very same character, used just as happily for the loose soil that earth breaks down into.

meaning_mnemonic: This one is a freebie, since the <radical>mountain</radical> radical and the <kanji>mountain</kanji> kanji are the exact same character.

meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>river</radical> radical and the <kanji>river</kanji> kanji are the same character, drawn as the same three flowing strokes every single time.

meaning_mnemonic: One flat <radical>ground</radical> line laid above the arms of the <radical>big</radical> outstretched person turns everything higher than it into <kanji>heaven</kanji>.

cast: き: Kiki, the tree spirit

It rockets out past your ear going <reading>じ</reading>, and all you manage is a weak <reading>gee</reading>. Every cat on the mossy steps now watches that rope instead of sleeping.

cast: こう: Koichi, the konbini king

reading_mnemonic: Every dawn the station guard sees the same tired man and sighs, <reading>Kai, you</reading> again. Kai rides the same train to the same desk daily, and that worn daily trip is 「<reading>かよう</reading>」, <vocabulary form="通う">to commute</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="通">traffic</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary> word are the same word. With this ending it just means something moves along the road and out the far side on its own, with nobody pushing it.
reading_mnemonic: The <reading>toll</reading>-gate guard lifts the barrier for one more truck and it rolls straight past him into the dark. A thing that goes in one side of a gap and out the far side on its own is 「<reading>とおる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="通る">to pass through</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Leave water still in the cold long enough and it turns hard and <kanji form="凍">frozen</kanji> all by itself. Water going solid like that, with nobody freezing it, is <vocabulary form="凍る">to freeze</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: At the garden pond a girl named <reading>Cora</reading> leaves her hose in the water overnight, and by dawn it sits locked in a clear block she cannot bend. Water setting hard and still on its own like that is 「<reading>こおる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="凍る">to freeze</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Drop a sugar cube into hot tea and stir once. It loses its edges, goes cloudy, and spreads through the water until it is gone, and that is what <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary> looks like.
reading_mnemonic: A chocolate coin left on the sunny windowsill goes from a hard <reading>token</reading> to a brown smear across the paint by noon. Something firm turning soft and runny with nobody touching it is 「<reading>とける</reading>」, <vocabulary form="溶ける">to melt / dissolve</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Shove a tub of rice to the back of the fridge and forget it for three weeks. The smell hits before you see the domed, slimy lid, and food left to turn that far is what <vocabulary form="腐る">to rot / spoil</vocabulary> means.
reading_mnemonic: A bowl of <reading>couscous</reading> left on the counter through a hot week goes grey, then furry, then sharp enough to drive everyone out of the kitchen. Food breaking down on its own like that is 「<reading>くさる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="腐る">to rot / spoil</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The side door is propped open a crack, and by the time the guard turns back the cell is empty. Getting clear through a gap before anyone can stop you is what it means <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: <reading>Nigel</reading> the gerbil works a bar of his cage loose every night and is halfway down the hall before the lights come on. A small thing bolting for the gap the moment it opens is 「<reading>にげる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="逃げる">to escape / run away</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A bun rolls off the bakery shelf and a boy runs after it down three aisles, hands out, never quite closing the gap. Staying right behind a thing that will not stop, trying to catch it, is what it means <vocabulary form="追いかける">to chase</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The keeper yells <reading>oi</reading> as a <reading>cackling</reading> hyena tears after the loose goat, staying one stride off its tail the whole length of the pen. That noisy pursuit, right behind and never letting up, is 「<reading>おいかける</reading>」, <vocabulary form="追いかける">to chase</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The host holds out the good sweets and you put a flat hand over your cup and say no until she takes the plate back. Turning down what someone offers, out loud and on purpose, is what it means <vocabulary form="断る">to refuse / decline</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Offered a pillow of <reading>cotton wool</reading> for the long ride, the old man shakes his head and sits bolt upright for four hours instead. Pushing back a thing you are handed, plainly and on purpose, is 「<reading>ことわる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="断る">to refuse / decline</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: You catch your neighbour at the gate, hold out your spare key, and ask her to feed the cat while you are gone. Putting a task in someone else's hands and counting on them to do it is what it means <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail you feed the lone vending machine your last coins and say <reading>ta</reading> before it even answers. It only hums, so you ask again, staking the whole climb on that one machine working, and that is 「<reading>たのむ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="頼む">to request / rely on</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="助">help</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary> word are the same. This ending flips it around so the help lands on you, and you are the one pulled clear, not the one doing the pulling.
reading_mnemonic: You go through the ice at the riverbank and a walrus hooks both <reading>tusks</reading> under your arms and heaves you onto the bank. Being lifted clear by something outside you, with no effort of your own, is 「<reading>たすかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="助かる">to be saved / helped</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A kid tips a full tray of paint across the floor, and the teacher kneels down and tells him in a hard, flat voice that this was not okay. Speaking to someone that sharply about what they did wrong is what it means <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Each wrong answer earns one more tap of <reading>chalk</reading> on the desk while the teacher lists your mistakes in a rising voice. That steady, sharp correction for a fault is 「<reading>しかる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="叱る">to scold</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Your kid brings home a drawing, and you pin it on the fridge, point to the careful shading, and tell her it is genuinely good. Saying plainly to someone that what they made is good is how you <vocabulary form="褒める">praise</vocabulary> them.
reading_mnemonic: A small kid on the little-league team finally connects and puts one over the fence, and the whole bench swarms him for the <reading>home run</reading>. Loading that kind of open approval onto someone for a job well done is 「<reading>ほめる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="褒める">to praise</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: You back your bike into a parked car, wince at the fresh scratch, and go knock on the owner's door to say sorry and offer to pay. Owning that you did wrong and saying so to the person is what it means <vocabulary form="謝る">to apologize</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: <reading>A llama</reading> at the petting zoo spits across the fence onto a boy's jacket, then drops its head and shuffles as if it knows it went too far. Admitting a wrong to the person you wronged, out loud, is 「<reading>あやまる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="謝る">to apologize</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Hand someone the news they have been hoping for and watch them <kanji form="喜">rejoice</kanji>, all grin and thank-yous and a little bounce. That whole warm rush when something goes right for you is being <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">pleased</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Koichi slides <reading>your cocoa</reading> across the konbini counter on the cold morning you needed it most, and you light up before it lands. That instant lift when a good thing reaches your hands is 「<reading>よろこぶ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="喜ぶ">to be pleased</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Someone slides into the parking spot you waited ten minutes for and smirks at you through the glass. Your face goes hot, your voice climbs, and that sudden flare of temper is what it means <vocabulary form="怒る">to get angry</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: One slice of slippery <reading>okra</reading> slides across your plate into the rice, and that alone is enough to tighten your jaw and ruin the meal. Heat rising in you over something that small is 「<reading>おこる</reading>」, <vocabulary form="怒る">to get angry</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: You have two job offers and one week to pick, and every night you lie awake running the same lists. Turning a hard choice over and over until it wears a groove in you is <vocabulary form="悩む">to worry / agonize</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Facing a call he cannot make, the man sits on the step and <reading>gnaws a yam</reading> raw, one slow bite at a time, staring at nothing. Working at a problem that will not come loose like that is 「<reading>なやむ</reading>」, <vocabulary form="悩む">to worry / agonize</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: You lift a plant pot to move it and the whole underside is crawling with woodlice spilling out at once. The jump in your chest and the step back you take before you can think is being <vocabulary form="驚く">surprised</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: You tip up what looks like an <reading>odd rock</reading> by the step and it opens into a crab and runs across your foot. You are standing before you have decided to move, and that jolt at a thing you did not expect is 「<reading>おどろく</reading>」, <vocabulary form="驚く">to be surprised</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: After the storm the old farmer stands in the flattened field and says the same low words about the lost year, over and over, to no one. Letting that grief out loud like that is what it means <vocabulary form="嘆く">to lament</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: <reading>A gecko</reading> on the shrine wall lets out a long, creaking wail every dusk over the moths it can no longer reach. Crying that kind of grief openly into the air is 「<reading>なげく</reading>」, <vocabulary form="嘆く">to lament</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Do the same small thing every day and the odd feeling fades on its own. Once it is completely gone, you have <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it.
reading_mnemonic: A <reading>nurse</reading> barely reacts to the sight of blood any more. Years on the ward mean she has completely <vocabulary form="慣れる">gotten used to</vocabulary> it, and that flat shrug is <reading>なれる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="経">pass through</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="経つ">for time to pass</vocabulary> word are the same; the extra kana on the end just makes it something time does by itself.
reading_mnemonic: On the mountain trail a hiker misses the last bus and <reading>tuts</reading> at his watch while the daylight fades. Each tut marks another minute <vocabulary form="経つ">passing</vocabulary> with nothing to fill it, and that slow drip is <reading>たつ</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Anything that slides past the mark it was meant to stop at, and keeps sliding, has <vocabulary form="過ぎる">passed or exceeded</vocabulary> it.
reading_mnemonic: Koichi keeps tipping <reading>sugar</reading> into one coffee and will not stop at two spoons or at ten. The level <vocabulary form="過ぎる">passes</vocabulary> every sane limit, and that pour that never quits is <reading>すぎる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Bow your head, close your eyes, and quietly ask a power you cannot see to keep someone safe. That asking, with nothing but words, is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: At dawn a line of pilgrims kneels in one long <reading>row</reading> on the shrine steps, foreheads to the stone, each asking an unseen power for rain. Kneeling in a <reading>row</reading> and begging like that is to <vocabulary form="祈る">pray</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いのる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Good news lands, so you deliberately gather people, food and noise around the one it happened to. That staged happiness is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The team wins and Sei's whole class erupts, caps in the air, everyone shouting 'I <reading>wow</reading>' around a cake nobody planned. Making that much noise on purpose for one person is to <vocabulary form="祝う">celebrate</vocabulary>, which is <reading>いわう</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: A coat on a hook stays put with no one holding it, and an hour spent on a job slips by the same way. Either one just <vocabulary form="掛かる">hangs</vocabulary> there and takes the time it takes.
reading_mnemonic: Leave a taxi parked with its meter on and the fare climbs by itself; the longer the <reading>car</reading> waits, the more it owes. That cost stacking up with no one touching it is for something to <vocabulary form="掛かる">take</vocabulary>, and it is <reading>かかる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Loose sheets keep drifting down onto each other with no hand guiding them, and the stack grows <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> as each one lands. Left to themselves they <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary> and settle into a pile.
reading_mnemonic: A dancer clacks her <reading>castanets</reading>, and the beats stack so fast they land on top of one another with no gap between them. Sounds falling onto sounds like that is to <vocabulary form="重なる">overlap</vocabulary>, or <reading>かさなる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: You bend low and aim your words at the floor near an important person's feet, so they reach that person from below. Speaking from down there, kept small on purpose, is to <vocabulary form="申す">say something humbly</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A tiny office <reading>mouse</reading> stands at the boardroom table and reports the figures in a voice so meek the directors lean right in. That head-down way of getting a word out is <vocabulary form="申す">to say something, humbly</vocabulary>, and it squeaks out as <reading>もうす</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: A servant finishes every task before anyone notices it needed doing, then sweeps away their own footprints so no one sees the work. Getting the whole job done while keeping yourself invisible is to <vocabulary form="致す">do it, humbly</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Two overalled helpers answer every call at the back door with a soft <reading>it's us</reading>, then quietly fix whatever broke and slip out again. Doing the work for someone while staying that far in the background is <vocabulary form="致す">to do, humbly</vocabulary>, spoken as <reading>いたす</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: You leave the car at the gate and walk the last stretch up to the house on foot, hat held in both hands. Coming toward someone that plainly, on foot and uncovered, is to <vocabulary form="参る">come to them humbly</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: An old retainer waves away every offer of a ride, saying that walking to you in person is <reading>my rule</reading>, and sets off down the full length of the road. That slow arrival on your own two feet is <vocabulary form="参る">to go and come humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>まいる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: You knock softly and wait outside the doorway until someone waves you in, then lean your head through to put your question. Approaching a person's home and their attention that carefully is to <vocabulary form="伺う">visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A polite <reading>kangaroo</reading> props its paws on the garden fence and waits to be waved through before hopping in to ask after your health. Peeking in and raising a question that gently is <vocabulary form="伺う">to visit and ask humbly</vocabulary>, which comes out as <reading>うかがう</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: You take the gift in both hands and lift it up past your forehead, putting yourself lower than the thing you were just given. Receiving or eating anything from that bowed-under position is to <vocabulary form="頂く">receive it, humbly</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: At the shrine a tame duck waddles up and drops a rice cracker into your cupped hands, and you bow lower than the bird to take it. That <reading>eat a duck</reading> moment, receiving with your head down, is <vocabulary form="頂く">to receive and eat, humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>いただく</reading>.

cast: か: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow
meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
reading_mnemonic: Once the runaway goat is <reading>collared</reading> and leashed, it <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> to you from right across the field. A goat you can call back in like that is <reading>こられる</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower and the motor goes quiet for good under your hands. Ending a running thing on purpose like that is what it means <vocabulary form="殺す">to kill</vocabulary> it.
reading_mnemonic: The frog <reading>chorus</reading> at the riverbank drones so flat and so long that it could <vocabulary form="殺す">kill</vocabulary> every houseplant on the windowsill. A sound that deadly is <reading>ころす</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: Tip up the old flowerpot by the back step and the packed soil under it comes alive with tiny legs and feelers that pour away from the daylight. Every scurrying speck down there is an <vocabulary form="虫">insect / bug</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Leave a peach on Koichi's counter until it turns <reading>mushy</reading>, and by morning the soft brown patch is crawling with every kind of <vocabulary form="虫">insect / bug</vocabulary>. Koichi flicks them off and mutters 「<reading>むし</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: A grey shape drops onto the trailhead vending machine, pops the flap with quick clever fingers and swings back up a pine with a stolen can. Only a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> robs a machine like that.
reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> snatches <reading>a sarong</reading> off the drying line and wears it up a tree. The washer-woman shakes her fist and yells 「<reading>さる</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: The animal that walks over to the paddock fence stands taller than you at the shoulder, long-faced, with a mane down its neck and a sweeping tail. That shape and size is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A toddler on the trail points at the animal being led past and gasps <reading>ooh, ma</reading> at her mother. The thing she means is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>, and the word she wants is 「<reading>うま</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="牛">cow</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they mean the same thing.
reading_mnemonic: The dairy farmer leans on the gate watching his best milker chew and sighs that <reading>ooh, she</reading> is a fine one. The animal he means is a <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary>, and he calls her 「<reading>うし</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini the scraps bin lies tipped over, and a fat pink animal stands in the spill with its snout down, grunting as it eats. Nothing empties a bin like a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The farmer fattens the animal every night on a bucket of <reading>butter</reading> and kitchen scraps until it can barely walk. That round, greasy thing is a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>, and he calls it 「<reading>ぶた</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="羊">sheep</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same animal.
reading_mnemonic: The shepherd sends her dog with one command, <reading>hit, Suzy</reading>, and it circles the woolly flock and drives them through the gate. Each fat woolly one is a <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary>, called 「<reading>ひつじ</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: At dusk a low red-brown shape slips along the treeline by the school field, quick and quiet, a white-tipped tail held straight out behind. That build and that tail mean a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The raider picks the coop latch every night and leaves it closed so tidily the farmer blames himself. <reading>Kit, so neat</reading> a thief has to be a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>, and the word is 「<reading>きつね</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: The beekeeper finds three hives smashed flat, the honey frames licked clean and claw marks gouged deep in the wood. Only a <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary> robs hives like that.
reading_mnemonic: Curled asleep in the hollow log, the animal is a perfect furry <reading>comma</reading>, nose tucked to tail. Nudge that 「<reading>くま</reading>」 awake and it unrolls into a very large <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The hose coiled on the riverbank path lifts one end, flicks a thin forked tongue, and pours itself smoothly off into the long grass. A rope that moves on its own is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A hiker nudges what looks like a <reading>heavy</reading> length of rope lying across the trail, and it coils back on itself and hisses. Rope that fights back is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>, 「<reading>へび</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: You step off the porch at dawn and walk face-first through a wide sticky net strung across the doorway. Sitting dead centre with its legs spread is the <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary> that spun it overnight.
reading_mnemonic: Mo walks the mountain trail into the same face-height web every dawn and yells <reading>come, Mo</reading> at nobody. The weaver that keeps rebuilding it is a <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary>, 「<reading>くも</reading>」.

cast: か: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow
meaning_mnemonic: The high thin whine circles your ear in the dark, stops, and a second later a hot itch rises on your arm. The thing that bit you and left that whine is a <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kaa</reading> the crow snaps at the whining speck by the power line, breathes one puff of flame, and swallows it charred. What she just ate was a <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary>, and her caw after is 「<reading>か</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: You set the bowl down for one minute and three of them already crowd the rim, rubbing their legs and testing the food. Nothing finds a meal faster than a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly (insect)</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The farmhand forks over the <reading>hay</reading> pile and a grey cloud lifts off it buzzing, then drops straight back down. Every dot in that cloud is a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly (insect)</vocabulary>, 「<reading>はえ</reading>」.

meaning_mnemonic: Out on the open sea the water never settles; it stacks itself into a moving ridge, throws that ridge at the land, then draws back to build the next. Each moving ridge is a <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Nami the lifeguard names every <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary> after herself. She stands on her tower shouting <reading>なみ</reading> at each wall of water as it rolls in, and the sound <reading>Nami</reading> has meant wave on that beach ever since.

meaning_mnemonic: The single character <kanji>forest</kanji> is the entire word, nothing added and nothing dropped. What you met as a kanji and what you say out loud as <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> are the same thing.
reading_mnemonic: Walk into the <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> and a mole named <reading>Morrie</reading> shoves his head up between two roots. He insists <reading>もり</reading> is his family name, since he dug every tunnel under these trees.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="林">grove</kanji> kanji you have already met and the <vocabulary form="林">woods / grove</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they carry the same meaning.
reading_mnemonic: A forest ranger named <reading>Hayashi</reading> has replanted the same <vocabulary form="林">woods / grove</vocabulary> three times after three separate fires. The locals gave up on the map name and just call the trees <reading>はやし</reading> after him.

meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="池">pond</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary> word are the same character, so of course they mean exactly the same thing.
reading_mnemonic: The <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary> behind Grandma Kane's shrine turns green and <reading>icky</reading> every August, thick enough to float a fallen leaf on top. The cats pick their way around it and she just calls it <reading>いけ</reading> and tops it up.

meaning_mnemonic: A single stone in the field is too big to lift, too heavy to roll, and was sitting there before the farm was. A stone that large and that settled is a <vocabulary form="岩">rock / boulder</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail swears the biggest <vocabulary form="岩">rock / boulder</vocabulary> up there is shaped exactly like the state of <reading>Iowa</reading>. Everyone else just calls it <reading>いわ</reading> and keeps climbing.

meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary form="砂">Sand</vocabulary> is what a cliff turns into after the sea grinds at it for a few thousand years. What is left is a pile of grains so small they run through your fingers and still will not brush off.
reading_mnemonic: A cat drags a whole <reading>tuna</reading> onto the beach and pats it down under the <vocabulary form="砂">sand</vocabulary> to save for later. By evening it has forgotten which stretch of <reading>すな</reading> holds the fish.

meaning_mnemonic: Mix plain dirt with enough rain and you get <vocabulary form="泥">mud</vocabulary>, a brown paste thick enough to hold a footprint and sticky enough to pull a boot off the foot that made it.
reading_mnemonic: Doro the farmhand goes to fetch water and comes back wearing half the riverbank, brown to the elbows with <vocabulary form="泥">mud</vocabulary>. Now one look at anyone in that state and the village just sighs <reading>どろ</reading>, said exactly like <reading>Doro</reading>.

meaning_mnemonic: When something burns, part of it leaves as a grey cloud that climbs, spreads flat under the ceiling, and stings your eyes. That rising grey cloud off a fire is <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The cook who trips the alarm most days insists the <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary> is just him working from <reading>memory</reading>. The fire crew now radio <reading>けむり</reading> before he has even lit the stove.

meaning_mnemonic: Strike a match and a small pointed shape of light stands up on the tip, orange at the edges and bluish at the base. That upright, leaning tongue of burning light is a <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A knight promises to guard the temple <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary> with his <reading>honor</reading> and never let it die. He falls asleep, it dies, and the other knights have whispered <reading>ほのお</reading> at him ever since.

meaning_mnemonic: Water held cold enough for long enough stops behaving like a liquid and turns hard, clear and slippery. Water in that solid state is <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: An old ice-cutter shows visitors where his crew once sawed winter <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary> from the lake in blocks, working it like a stone <reading>quarry</reading>. He still calls that frozen lake <reading>こおり</reading>, the word his crew used for the place.

meaning_mnemonic: Sometimes the wind, the rain, the black cloud and the noise all arrive together and stay for a whole day. A whole sky misbehaving at once is a <vocabulary form="嵐">storm</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The kanji here means <kanji form="苦">suffering</kanji>, and suffering on the tongue is exactly what <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary> is. The い on the end marks it as a describing word.
reading_mnemonic: Nigel the goat gnaws lemon rind and raw dandelion stalks, pulls a long face, and calls every mouthful <reading>にがい</reading> — <reading>Nigel</reading>'s one word for <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The pucker that grabs both cheeks when you bite a lemon wedge by mistake is <vocabulary form="酸っぱい">sour</vocabulary>. The い ending marks it as a describing word.
reading_mnemonic: Dinner is a <reading>supper pie</reading> that has turned in the heat, and one forkful folds your face in half — <reading>すっぱい</reading>, the taste we call <vocabulary form="酸っぱい">sour</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A heavy dish sits over a flame in the middle of the table, and everyone drops in cabbage and tofu and fishes it back out. That dish, and the shared meal made in it, is a <vocabulary form="鍋">pot / hotpot</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Cut the price into equal <kanji form="割">proportion</kanji>s, then <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> a few of those parts away before you pay. The parts pulled off the total are the <vocabulary form="割引">discount</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A hard bark of air fires up your throat with no warning and rattles the whole quiet room. That sharp, helpless burst is a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Koichi tears open a <reading>sack</reading> of flour at the konbini and breathes the white cloud straight in. It punches out a <reading>せき</reading> loud enough to stop the beeping till, because a chestful of flour always ends in a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Pull a <kanji form="邪">wicked</kanji> <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> deep into your chest and let it settle in as a three-day fever. Drawing bad air right inside you like that is what it means <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A cold gust off the river hooks Kaz like a fish on a line and reels him straight into bed. When chilled air <reading>hooks</reading> into you and holds on, that is <reading>かぜをひく</reading>, <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.

cast: と: Toto, the door-to-door turtle

meaning_mnemonic: Dodging a slash aimed at your heart is not a choice your body makes. It happens every time because the move is <kanji form="必">necessary</kanji>, and something that locked-in happens <vocabulary form="必ず">definitely / without fail</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Kana the courier has never missed one delivery, in storms or on holidays. The way <reading>Kana rushes</reading> it out every single time is <reading>かならず</reading>, <vocabulary form="必ず">definitely / without fail</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: To pin down what 'a bird' means you hold up one sparrow and one crow and let those two stand in for the whole idea. Reaching for a specific case to carry the general one is <vocabulary form="例えば">for example</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: The artist at the <reading>tattoo bar</reading> never describes a style in words. She flips to one drawing, says <reading>たとえば</reading> this dragon, and lets that single sample do the defining, which is <vocabulary form="例えば">for example</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: Whatever option you pick, this person's <kanji form="構">stance</kanji> does not shift even slightly. A body that stays relaxed no matter what you choose is telling you <vocabulary form="構いません">it doesn't matter</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A stalk you raised yourself, coming up green through your own patch of earth, is the small sure <kanji form="幸">happiness</kanji> of being <vocabulary form="幸せ">happy / fortunate</vocabulary>. It works as a な adjective, so な sits before the noun.
reading_mnemonic: The woman on the bench gives a small wave at nothing whenever her luck turns. That reflex, <reading>she waves</reading>, is <reading>しあわせ</reading>, the tell of someone <vocabulary form="幸せ">happy / fortunate</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: The first desk inside the door <kanji form="受">accepts</kanji> your name and <kanji form="付">attaches</kanji> you to the person you came to see. That desk is the <vocabulary form="受付">reception (desk)</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: A bowing front-desk clerk greets every visitor with the same line: 「OK, <reading>take a key</reading>.」 Blur those words together and you hear <reading>うけつけ</reading>, the <vocabulary form="受付">reception (desk)</vocabulary> where everyone checks in.

meaning_mnemonic: A scrap of land with open sea on every side of it, no bridge and no road off, is an <vocabulary form="島">island</vocabulary>.

meaning_mnemonic: A view that is nothing but flooded <kanji form="田">rice paddy</kanji> and one lonely <kanji form="舎">hut</kanji> at its edge is the <vocabulary form="田舎">countryside</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Nao the delivery gecko groans that every run out here means three hours <reading>in a car</reading>. That long haul to 「<reading>いなか</reading>」 is just what visiting the <vocabulary form="田舎">countryside</vocabulary> costs.

meaning_mnemonic: A village <kanji form="祭">ritual</kanji> for the local gods, once the whole street piles on food stalls, drums and lanterns, has grown into a <vocabulary form="祭り">festival</vocabulary>.
reading_mnemonic: Tomo the tanuki knows the shrine <reading>mats really</reading> fill up fast once the drums start. He stakes out his spot for the 「<reading>まつり</reading>」 hours before the <vocabulary form="祭り">festival</vocabulary> begins.
